newsitem.title: CANADA: FORECAST-Canada housing starts set for sharp rise.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Canada housing starts set for sharp rise.

text.p: Housing construction in Canada is poised for two years of strong growth, powered by pent-up consumer demand and some of the lowest interest rates in 40 years, according to a Reuters poll.
The quarterly Reuters survey, which polled 22 economists in Canada and the United States, found housing starts are expected to increase in each quarter of 1997 and the first three quarters of 1998.

"What people are expecting is that as the economy improves over 1997 confidence will increase and people will make the plunge. I think we're starting to see evidence of that," said Rick Egelton, deputy chief economist with Bank of Montreal.

According to the survey, economists expect housing starts to rise from a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 138,500 in the first quarter of 1997 to 149,200 by the fourth quarter of 1997. Housing starts are seen rising further next year, reaching 158,700 by the fourth quarter of 1998.
Expectations of a steady boom in housing construction stem from several factors, the most important of which is interest rates, analysts said.

Prime lending rates at Canada's major chartered banks, currently at 4.75 percent, are at their lowest since March, 1956. Low prime and mortgage lending rates are the product of an aggressive easing campaign by the Bank of Canada, which has cut rates by a total of 500 basis points since May, 1995 in a bid to spur a sluggish economy.

Most analysts believe Canada is now at the bottom of the interest rate cycle and the next move by the Bank of Canada will be a rate hike. As a result consumers are expected to take advantage of the lower rates.

"Low interest rates are finally beginning to have an impact on the housing market. We saw in 1996 the big rebound in sales of existing homes. Now we're moving on to starts," said Carlos Leitao, an economist with Royal Bank of Canada.
A "significant" amount of pent-up demand among consumers is also expected to drive housing starts higher over the next two years, economists said.

While the growth in housing starts may appear impressive, it somes off a low base. Housing starts tumbled to 30-year lows in the early 1990s, analysts said. An improving economy and lower rates are only now beginning to lure consumers back into the market.

"If you take the pent-up demand that's required, take the tremendous improvement we've seen in housing affordability, and that translates into a fairly bullish housing market," said Bank of Montreal's Egelton.
He said housing affordability has now reached levels not seen since the early 1970's, providing a strong incentive for consumers to build homes.

The only potential threat to the expected housing boom stems from the same factor that prompted it -- interest rates. While a rise in rates appears unlikely at this point, such a move would halt a housing starts recovery in its tracks.

"The most important risk that one can see is on the interest rate side. If one were to see a sudden spike in interest rates that could have a negative impact on consumer confidence," said Leitao. "That would be the factor to keep an eye on."
